newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, S.Korea trapped again in World War Two quagmire.
newsitem.headline: Japan, S.Korea trapped again in World War Two quagmire.

text.p: Japan and South Korea found themselves trapped again in the quagmire of World War Two during a weekend summit that highlighted increasing frustration in both countries at their inability to leave behind the past.

The summit of two free-market democracies and powerful U.S. surrogates in Asia, meant to show a united front to growing Chinese economic power and North Korean militarism, turned into a catfight over Japan's World War Two actions.

Japan's top government spokesman lit the fuse on the eve of Saturday's meeting when he said there was a "social background" to the Japanese military's use of sex slaves, or "comfort women," in frontline brothels during World War Two.
About 200,000 captured "comfort women" from Korea, the Philippines, China, Indonesia and the Netherlands were forced into prostitution in one of World War Two's darker chapters.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was immediately on the defensive and forced to make an apology to South Korean President Kim Young-sam in the opening minutes of the summit.

Japanese analysts said it was an all-too-familiar scenario -- insensitive comments by a Japanese politician and an overreaction by South Korean public opinion getting in the way of improving ties between two nations with the same interests.

In Seoul, South Korean newspapers expressed dismay at the summit results, saying it had failed to heal old wounds. The meeting was faulted for treading lightly over the sex slave issue and a territorial dispute over two small islands.
Even Kim, the aggrieved party, indicated at a news conference with Hashimoto at the end of the summit that it was time the two countries overcame their endless bickering.
"We can't hide and erase what happened in the past and we must develop our future while looking at the past," he said.
But, he added: "There were disputes among European Union members and Association of Southeast Asian Nations members, but they overcame them to achieve harmony. We can take lessons from them."

Masao Okonogi, professor of Asian studies at Tokyo's Keio University, said Tokyo and Seoul were bound together by nervousness about China's growing might as well as communist North Korea's militarism and possible collapse.
"We both should put the past behind us," he told Reuters. "Yet when the two countries take off their masks, you always see these (World War Two) sticking points."

Nozomu Akizuki, professor of East Asian diplomacy at Tokai University, believes South Korea, as a Confucian nation, cannot accept Japan's constant argument that all issues were settled when it took the legal step of signing a 1952 Peace Treaty in San Francisco.
"In South Korea, whose tradition is firmly based on Confucianism, people don't make any distinction between law and morality. That's the basic difference," Akizuki told Reuters.

Some analysts said there appeared to be a growing mood in even some parts of mainstream Japan that after three successive prime ministers, including Hashimoto, have apologised for World War Two, no more gesture of contrition is needed.

"I always complain to people of my parent's generation that that they took too long and did not act quickly enough to acknowledge Japan's past," a 41-year-old businessman visiting Beppu during the summit said.

"But now 50 years later is there anything more persuasive that we can do. I hate to see Japan always being looked at as a villain by its Asian neighbours," said the man, who did not want to be identified.
